notes.definition: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is a non-communicable disease in which layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
explanation: The heart muscle needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose for respiration, delivered by the coronary arteries. In coronary heart disease, fatty material (largely cholesterol) builds up in layers in the walls of these arteries. The lumen becomes narrower, so less blood flows to the heart muscle. Without enough oxygen the muscle cannot respire aerobically, causing chest pain. If an artery becomes completely blocked, for example by a blood clot forming on the fatty deposit, part of the heart muscle dies, which is a heart attack.

Stents are used to keep coronary arteries open. A stent is a small mesh tube. It is inserted using a catheter with a balloon, guided to the narrowed section and expanded by inflating the balloon. The stent stays in place and holds the artery open, restoring blood flow. Stents work quickly and need only minor surgery with a short recovery, but there is a risk of complications during surgery, of infection and of a blood clot forming near the stent (thrombosis), and fatty material can build up again.

Statins are drugs widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit. They reduce the risk of CHD and can increase the level of 'good' cholesterol. However, they must be taken for life, take time to work, and can have side effects such as muscle pain or liver problems. Some people forget to take them regularly.

In some people heart valves may become faulty, preventing the valve from opening fully, or the valve might develop a leak. A leaky valve allows blood to flow backwards, so less blood is pumped forward with each beat and the heart has to work harder; the person may become breathless and tired. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological valves (from animals such as pigs or cows, or from human donors) or mechanical valves. Mechanical valves last a long time but require lifelong anti-clotting drugs; biological valves do not need these drugs but wear out sooner.

In the case of heart failure, a donor heart, or heart and lungs together, can be transplanted. Donors are in short supply, the patient must take immunosuppressant drugs for life to prevent rejection, and there are risks from major surgery. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive while they wait for a transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery. They are less likely to be rejected because they are made of materials that do not trigger an immune response, but they can cause blood clots and the patient must take anti-clotting drugs.

You need to be able to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of treating cardiovascular diseases by drugs, mechanical devices or transplant. A good evaluation weighs effectiveness, risk, cost, side effects, availability and whether lifestyle changes would also be needed, and ends with a justified conclusion.
keyFacts: In CHD, layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them.
Narrowed coronary arteries reduce blood flow, causing a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
Stents are mesh tubes that keep coronary arteries open.
Statins reduce blood cholesterol, slowing the rate at which fatty material is deposited.
Faulty valves may not open fully or may leak, allowing backflow.
Faulty valves can be replaced with biological or mechanical valves.
In heart failure, a donor heart or heart and lungs can be transplanted.
Artificial hearts can keep patients alive until a transplant, or let the heart rest to recover.
Transplant patients need immunosuppressant drugs to reduce the risk of rejection.
Mechanical valves and artificial hearts need anti-clotting drugs.

keyTerms.definition: A disease in which fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
Arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood.
A small mesh tube inserted into an artery to hold it open.
A drug that lowers blood cholesterol, slowing the build-up of fatty material in arteries.
A fatty substance in the blood; high levels increase the rate of fatty deposits in arteries.
A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
An immune response in which the body attacks a transplanted organ as foreign.
A drug that suppresses the immune system to reduce the risk of rejection of a transplant.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change in cholesterol
workedExamples.question: A patient's blood cholesterol fell from 6.4 mmol/dm³ to 4.8 mmol/dm³ after taking statins. Calculate the percentage decrease.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating stents and statins
workedExamples.question: Evaluate the use of a stent compared with statins for a patient whose coronary artery is already 80% blocked.
steps: Stent: immediately widens the artery and restores blood flow; minor surgery; short recovery. Risks: infection, blood clot, artery can narrow again.
Statins: no surgery; slow further build-up of fatty material over time. Disadvantages: do not remove existing blockage; must be taken for life; possible side effects.
Conclusion: because the artery is already severely narrowed, a stent is the better immediate treatment, with statins taken afterwards to reduce further build-up.
workedExamples.answer: A stent is more suitable for an existing severe blockage, with statins as a long-term addition.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think CHD is caused by fat building up inside the heart chambers.
misconceptions.right: In fact the fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle itself.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think statins remove existing fatty deposits.
misconceptions.right: In fact statins lower blood cholesterol, which slows down the rate of further fatty deposits; they do not clear existing blockages.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the heart muscle stops because it runs out of blood in the chambers.
misconceptions.right: In fact heart muscle is damaged because it lacks oxygen for aerobic respiration when its coronary arteries are narrowed or blocked.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mechanical valves and artificial hearts are rejected like donor organs.
misconceptions.right: In fact they are made of materials that do not trigger an immune response, so rejection is not the main problem; the main risk is blood clots.

realWorld: Coronary heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in the UK and worldwide.
Many adults over 40 in the UK are prescribed statins to reduce their risk of heart attacks and strokes.
Pig heart valves are commonly used as biological replacement valves.
Artificial hearts have kept patients alive for months or years while they wait for a donor heart.
examTips: Say 'fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries', not 'in the heart', and link it to less oxygen for heart muscle.
For 'evaluate' questions, give advantages AND disadvantages of each treatment and finish with a justified conclusion.
Remember which treatment needs which drugs: transplants need immunosuppressants; mechanical valves and artificial hearts need anti-clotting drugs.
When explaining the effect of a leaky valve, mention backflow of blood and less oxygenated blood reaching the body.
summary: CHD: fatty material narrows the coronary arteries, reducing oxygen to heart muscle.
Stents hold arteries open; statins lower cholesterol and slow fatty deposits.
Faulty valves can be replaced with biological or mechanical valves.
Heart failure can be treated by heart or heart and lung transplant.
Artificial hearts keep patients alive until a transplant or let the heart rest.
Each treatment has advantages and disadvantages that must be weighed.

questions.question: In coronary heart disease, where does fatty material build up?
questions.explanation: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle; they become narrowed by fatty deposits.

questions.question: What is a stent?
options: A mesh tube that holds an artery open
An electrical device that controls heart rate
questions.explanation: A stent is a mesh tube. Statins lower cholesterol and pacemakers control heart rate.

questions.question: What do statins do?
questions.explanation: Statins lower cholesterol, slowing the deposit of fatty material.

questions.question: Why does narrowing of the coronary arteries cause chest pain during exercise?
options: The heart chambers fill with fat
Heart muscle receives too little oxygen for its increased rate of respiration
Too much blood reaches the heart muscle
questions.explanation: During exercise heart muscle needs more oxygen. Narrow arteries cannot deliver enough.

questions.question: Which treatment requires the patient to take immunosuppressant drugs?
questions.explanation: A donor heart is foreign tissue and may be rejected by the immune system. The other treatments do not involve donor tissue from another person.

questions.question: What is a consequence of a leaking heart valve?
options: Blood flows backwards, so less blood is pumped forward with each beat
Blood pressure in the aorta increases
Cholesterol levels in the blood rise
questions.explanation: A leaky valve lets blood flow back into the chamber it came from, reducing the efficiency of the heart.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of a mechanical heart valve compared with a biological valve?
options: It is rejected by the immune system
The patient must take anti-clotting drugs for life
It can only be taken from pigs
questions.explanation: Mechanical valves increase clot risk, so lifelong anti-clotting drugs are needed. Biological valves wear out sooner.

questions.question: Why are artificial hearts unlikely to be rejected?
options: They contain the patient's own cells
They are made of materials that do not trigger an immune response
They are only fitted for a few hours
questions.explanation: Artificial hearts are made from materials such as plastics and metals that the immune system does not recognise as foreign antigens.

questions.question: A patient's coronary artery is 90% blocked and they are having frequent chest pain. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: A stent widens the artery immediately. Statins work slowly and do not remove existing blockage; transplant is for heart failure; a valve does not treat a narrowed artery.

questions.question: Why might a doctor fit an artificial heart in a patient who is not waiting for a transplant?
options: To allow the patient's own heart to rest and recover
To stop the immune system working
questions.explanation: Artificial hearts can be used temporarily to take over pumping so the patient's heart can rest.

questions.question: A patient's cholesterol level fell from 7.0 to 5.6 mmol/dm³ after taking statins. Calculate the percentage decrease.
A country records 520 000 deaths in one year. 1 in 8 of these deaths is caused by coronary heart disease. Calculate the number of deaths caused by CHD that year.
questions.explanation: 1 in 8 means divide by 8: 520 000 ÷ 8 = 65 000.

questions.question: The lumen of a healthy coronary artery has a diameter of 4.0 mm. Fatty material reduces the diameter to 2.0 mm. Calculate the percentage decrease in the cross-sectional area of the lumen. (Area of a circle = πr²)
questions.explanation: Halving the diameter halves the radius, and area depends on radius squared, so the area becomes one quarter: a 75% decrease. Saying 50% is the most common error.

questions.question: In a trial, 4.0% of patients taking a placebo had a heart attack within 5 years, compared with 2.8% of patients taking statins. Calculate the percentage reduction in risk for patients taking statins.
questions.explanation: The fall is 1.2 percentage points. As a proportion of the placebo risk this is 1.2 ÷ 4.0 = 0.30, a 30% reduction.

questions.question: A stent costs £1200 to fit. Statins cost £18 per year. How many years of statins cost the same as fitting one stent?
questions.explanation: 1200 ÷ 18 = 66.67 years. This shows that comparing costs is not straightforward; statins are cheap per year but are taken for life, while stents carry other costs such as hospital care.

questions.question: State one way a heart valve can become faulty.
markScheme: 1 mark: it may not open fully / it may develop a leak
questions.explanation: Both faults reduce the efficiency of the heart.

questions.question: Give two types of replacement heart valve.
markScheme: 1 mark: biological (from animals or human donors)
questions.explanation: Biological valves come from pigs, cows or human donors; mechanical valves are man-made.

questions.question: Explain how a build-up of fatty material in the coronary arteries can lead to a heart attack.
markScheme: 1 mark: the artery narrows / becomes blocked, reducing blood flow to heart muscle
1 mark: so heart muscle lacks oxygen and cannot respire, and the muscle is damaged or dies
questions.explanation: The chain is: fatty material → narrower lumen → less blood → less oxygen → muscle damage.

questions.question: Give one advantage and two disadvantages of using statins to treat coronary heart disease.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: reduce the risk of CHD / no surgery needed / can increase 'good' cholesterol
1 mark: disadvantage: must be taken long term / patient may forget
1 mark: disadvantage: side effects such as liver damage or muscle pain / take time to have an effect
questions.explanation: Statins are a drug treatment: non-invasive, but long-term with possible side effects.

questions.question: Describe how a stent is fitted into a narrowed coronary artery.
markScheme: 1 mark: a catheter carrying a deflated balloon and stent is passed into the narrowed artery
1 mark: the balloon is inflated, expanding the stent, then deflated and removed, leaving the stent holding the artery open
questions.explanation: The stent remains in the artery after the balloon is removed.

questions.question: Suggest why a patient who has a heart transplant is more likely to get infections.
markScheme: 1 mark: patient takes immunosuppressant drugs to prevent rejection
1 mark: these reduce the activity of the immune system / white blood cells
1 mark: so pathogens are less likely to be destroyed / patient cannot fight infections as effectively
questions.explanation: The drugs that stop rejection also weaken the defence against pathogens.

questions.question: A person has a leaky valve between the left atrium and left ventricle. Explain why they become breathless and tired easily.
markScheme: 1 mark: blood flows back into the left atrium when the ventricle contracts
1 mark: so less oxygenated blood is pumped into the aorta to the body
1 mark: so muscles receive less oxygen for aerobic respiration (and the heart works harder / person breathes faster)
questions.explanation: Linking backflow to less oxygen delivery and less aerobic respiration gives full marks.

questions.question: Give two reasons why a patient may have to wait a long time for a heart transplant.
markScheme: 1 mark: donor heart must be a close tissue match / correct size / blood group
questions.explanation: Donor hearts are scarce and must be compatible to reduce the risk of rejection.

questions.question: Which word describes the build-up in coronary heart disease?
questions.explanation: CHD is caused by layers of fatty material, not by an infection.

questions.question: Which treatment for heart failure is used to keep a patient alive while they wait for a donor heart?
questions.explanation: Artificial hearts take over pumping until a donor heart becomes available.

questions.question: Describe how coronary heart disease develops and how it affects the heart.
markScheme: Indicative content: coronary arteries supply oxygenated blood to heart muscle; fatty material (cholesterol) builds up in layers inside the coronary arteries; lumen narrows; blood flow to heart muscle reduced; heart muscle receives less oxygen (and glucose); less aerobic respiration; chest pain, especially during exercise; a blood clot may form and block the artery completely; part of the heart muscle dies (heart attack).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence from fatty build-up through narrowing and reduced blood flow to lack of oxygen for heart muscle and its consequences.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'arteries get blocked' with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use cause and effect connectives (so, which means) to show the sequence.

questions.question: A 58-year-old patient has coronary heart disease. Their doctor considers three treatments: statins, a stent, or a heart transplant if the heart fails. Evaluate these treatments.
markScheme: Indicative content: statins: advantages: no surgery, reduce cholesterol and slow further build-up, reduce risk of heart attack, cheap per dose; disadvantages: must be taken for life, side effects such as liver problems, take time to work, do not remove existing deposits. Stents: advantages: widen artery immediately, restore blood flow, minor surgery under local anaesthetic, short recovery; disadvantages: risk of infection, blood clot, artery may narrow again, surgical risk. Transplant: advantages: replaces a failing heart, can give many more years of life; disadvantages: major surgery, shortage of donors and long wait, lifelong immunosuppressant drugs, rejection risk, increased infections; only suitable for heart failure. Justified conclusion: for example a stent to restore blood flow combined with statins and lifestyle changes; transplant only if the heart fails.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): advantages and disadvantages of all three treatments with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): advantages and disadvantages of at least two treatments, conclusion may be missing or unjustified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant points about one or more treatments, mainly descriptive.
questions.explanation: An 'evaluate' question needs a conclusion. Without a justified judgement you cannot reach Level 3.
